n09.notes: Accurate and fully cited, with the worked example included. At 257 words it is well over the 150-word limit; the too-high and too-low SEL bullets and the speculative closing paragraph pad it.
n09.answer:
Specific edge load (SEL), also called refining intensity, is the net refining energy applied per unit length of bar crossing. It is normally expressed in watt-seconds per metre (Ws/m) [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.23] [DOC 856ff3f6-9be4-42e7-b4dc-fee63dfd3cfd p.34].

**Calculation**
- SEL = (applied motor power − no-load power) / (RPM × bar edge length × min/60 s) [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.23].
- No-load power is the hydraulic loss that heats the fluid but does no refining, so it is subtracted from motor load [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.23].
- Worked example in the manual: net 363 kW, bar edge length 30 km/rev, 600 rpm, which gives 1.2 Ws/m [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.41].

**Why recycled fiber needs a lower SEL**
- Higher SEL gives more shortened and cut fibers. Lower SEL gives more pronounced fibrillation. The recycling reference states "Recycling requires lower SEL" [DOC 856ff3f6-9be4-42e7-b4dc-fee63dfd3cfd p.34].
- Lower SEL also gives better properties. In the low-consistency refining curves, 500 Ws/km gave higher tensile and less tear loss than 1,500 Ws/km at the same energy [DOC 856ff3f6-9be4-42e7-b4dc-fee63dfd3cfd p.35].
- Too high an SEL causes severe fiber cutting, plate clashing, short plate life and poor strength development [DOC 856ff3f6-9be4-42e7-b4dc-fee63dfd3cfd p.36].
- Too low an SEL can leave fibers poorly developed and make the freeness drop inefficient [DOC 856ff3f6-9be4-42e7-b4dc-fee63dfd3cfd p.36].

The library does not say why recycled fiber in particular responds this way. The likely reason, from general engineering knowledge, is that recycled fibers have already been dried and refined once and are shorter and weaker. Gentle fibrillation develops bonding without cutting away the length they have left.

n10.notes: Accurate and fully cited. The seal-water paragraph was not asked for. The capacity-ratio definition is only implied ('compared with the manufacturer's curve'), and same speed is not mentioned.
n10.answer:
About $18,000 a year is wasted: 30% of the $60,000 energy cost.

The TAPPI procedure says a worn pump draws the same power as a new one while delivering less capacity [DOC a92ccac2-eca7-4b0a-a2cc-bd07d3da9fa5 p.3]. It gives the wasted energy cost as Equation 3, annual energy cost × (1 − % original capacity) [DOC a92ccac2-eca7-4b0a-a2cc-bd07d3da9fa5 p.4].

Calculation: $60,000 × (1 − 0.70) = $18,000 per year.

The same rule applies to seal water. About 30% of its cost is also wasted, using Equation 4 [DOC a92ccac2-eca7-4b0a-a2cc-bd07d3da9fa5 p.4]. That is on top of the $18,000.

The 70% figure should come from a capacity test at the optimum vacuum level for the application, compared with the manufacturer's curve [DOC a92ccac2-eca7-4b0a-a2cc-bd07d3da9fa5 p.3].

n12.notes: All points correct and cited. At 202 words it runs over the ~150-word target, with an unrequested uhle-box sizing bullet and a couch-marking caveat.
n12.answer:
A flatbox doesn't need more than five or six slots. Slot widths are usually reduced as the sheet gets closer to the couch [DOC 56ec08f5-d829-4786-b810-b1a7de9c7f74 p.4]. This comes from a general best-practice paper (Doug Sweet & Associates). It isn't specific to PM1.

Other ways to reduce table drive load, from the same source:
- Remove flatboxes you don't need. Boxes with too much slot area also go. The paper says there are often too many of both [DOC 56ec08f5-d829-4786-b810-b1a7de9c7f74 p.4].
- Use higher vacuum with less slot area. It describes this as improving dewatering while cutting power [DOC 56ec08f5-d829-4786-b810-b1a7de9c7f74 p.4].
- Rework the flatbox covers with low-drag ceramics such as silicon nitride [DOC 56ec08f5-d829-4786-b810-b1a7de9c7f74 p.4]. Together with the measures above, this can easily save 10–20% of power across the couch, wire turning roll and other former drives [DOC 56ec08f5-d829-4786-b810-b1a7de9c7f74 p.4].
- Size slot area by machine speed only. For example, 1" of total slot width is enough at 2500 fpm. More dwell time only adds vacuum pump capacity and power demand [DOC 56ec08f5-d829-4786-b810-b1a7de9c7f74 p.5]. That example is for uhle boxes.

Higher vacuum at the couch has limits. Couch marking is avoided by keeping solids high enough after the flatboxes [DOC 7d704e0a-0ca7-4284-8fb9-dc6721c03b8a p.12].

n11.notes: All MUST points covered and every citation is supported. At 201 words it runs over the ~150 target, with unrequested extras (Table I, AFT refining). The NICE point on high-yield/recycled fiber is missing.
n11.answer:
**Sheet density, which comes from fiber bonding, is the main control on linerboard compressive strength.** That is the library's main finding. The Institute of Paper Chemistry survey says density (fiber bonding) "is a major factor affecting compressive strength" [DOC 168553e0-baa3-4e06-827d-54415678796a p.4].

Supporting points from the same report:
- **Favoring factors:** High compressive strength is favored by higher density, high fiber compressive moduli and z-direction fiber orientation. Density matters mainly through its effect on fiber bonding [DOC 168553e0-baa3-4e06-827d-54415678796a p.5].
- **Fiber limit:** In well-bonded sheets, fiber modulus and strength may limit the ultimate edgewise compressive strength [DOC 168553e0-baa3-4e06-827d-54415678796a p.4].
- **Fiber type:** Stiff, thick, well-bonded fibers such as hardwoods favor compressive strength. It looks relatively insensitive to pulping yield at constant density [DOC 168553e0-baa3-4e06-827d-54415678796a p.4].
- **Papermaking factors:** Table I, taken from Koning and Haskell (Paperboard Packaging, 1979), lists wet pressing and freeness as the significant factors for compressive strength [DOC 168553e0-baa3-4e06-827d-54415678796a p.20].
- **Refining:** The AFT manual says compressive strength rises with refining in a nearly linear relationship to density [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.18].
- **Orientation and drying:** Fiber orientation and MD drying strain have opposing effects on MD and CD compressive strength. Linerboard needs high CD compressive strength [DOC 168553e0-baa3-4e06-827d-54415678796a p.5].
